extracted.intended_audience: claimants, respondents, representatives, and other participants in Copyright Claims Board (CCB) proceedings (including pro se parties and counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Final rule establishing procedures governing active proceedings before the Copyright Claims Board and post-determination procedures under the CASE Act, including party management, discovery, hearings, defaults, smaller-claims procedures, and publication/records rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility for pro se parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The CASE Act's legislative history states that the Office should establish a process that is “accessible especially for pro se parties and those with little prior formal exposure to copyright laws.” The CCB is designed to be accessible to pro se parties without formal legal training and others with little exposure to copyright law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To implement this goal, the Office will publish a user-friendly CCB Handbook written in easy-to-understand language, maintain a user-friendly electronic filing system (eCCB) with prompts and fillable forms to walk parties through claims/responses/counterclaims, and provide Copyright Claims Attorneys and other CCB staff to guide parties. The Office revised rules to simplify regulatory language and remove or simplify procedures where possible, while retaining necessary procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder and intervention (necessary parties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CASE Act requires dismissal of a claim for the failure to join a necessary party. The NPRM proposed a process for parties to bring the failure to join a necessary party to the CCB's attention and for non-parties to seek to intervene in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rule simplifies procedure for intervention by having requests and any responses filed via a simple form on eCCB. The CCB may hold a conference to discuss proposed intervention with parties and the intervenor. If a party requesting intervention is found to be a “necessary” party, claims will be dismissed if the parties do not consent to its addition or intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary withdrawal and dismissal of claims/counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may voluntarily dismiss their own claims or counterclaims without prejudice before a response is filed. A claim or counterclaim cannot be voluntarily dismissed after a response is filed, but the claimant or counterclaimant may request to withdraw the claim and the CCB will have discretion to dismiss with or without prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors the CCB will consider when exercising discretion include the point in the proceedings at which dismissal is requested and whether dismissal without prejudice is in the interests of justice. The CCB Handbook will explain terms like 'with prejudice' and 'without prejudice' in plain English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default determinations and missed-deadline cure process
rubrics_metrics.description: The CASE Act provides that the CCB may enter a default determination if “the respondent has failed to appear or has ceased participating in the proceeding.” Under the proposed rule, respondents that do not respond to CCB deadlines will receive an opportunity to cure the first two times they miss a deadline without cause; after the third missed deadline, the CCB may proceed to a default judgment in its discretion without giving another opportunity to cure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulation spells out procedural steps leading up to a default determination and steps after a request to vacate a default. When default is sought, the statute requires the CCB to “require the claimant to submit relevant evidence and other information in support of the claimant's claim and any asserted damages” and determine whether that evidence supports a finding of default. The Board shall consider whether the respondent has a meritorious defense; if a meritorious defense is apparent, the claimant's submissions must be sufficient under applicable law. Before finding for a defaulting respondent (i.e., denying a claimant's default), the CCB will provide a tentative ruling and an opportunity for the claimant to address it, including by submitting further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to prosecute (claimant-side cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adds a procedure allowing claimants a cure opportunity for failure to prosecute, similar to the cure opportunities provided to respondents for missed deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses commenter concerns that the original proposed regulations provided cures only for respondents. The added procedure permits restoration or other relief in the interests of fairness when claimants fail to pursue their claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad-faith conduct and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties and their representatives who engage in bad-faith conduct before the CCB may be required to pay reasonable costs and attorney's fees; upon repeated bad-faith acts they may be barred from participating in further proceedings for a year and have pending proceedings dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule adopts a broad conception of bad-faith conduct (including actions taken in support of a claim, counterclaim, or defense before the CCB). The CCB may act sua sponte or on a party's allegation. Accused parties will be notified and given an opportunity to respond in writing and at a conference. Illustrative examples of bad-faith conduct will appear in the CCB Handbook. The Office declined to publish a public list of bad-faith actors at this time but indicated that determinations will be public and eCCB will allow searches of related orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on number of proceedings (docket-management / anti-abuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office is authorized to limit the permitted number of proceedings each year by the same claimant and to limit the number of proceedings private attorneys or law firms may represent claimants in, to promote efficient administration and prevent abusive conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM proposed limits of 10 proceedings per claimant and 40 per private attorney/firm in any 12-month period; based on comments and concerns about foreclosing claimants who often face opt-outs, the final rule raised the claimant filing limit to 30 proceedings in a 12-month period. The Office retained authority to limit counsel filings as well (subject to comments and statutory interpretation). Limits apply to filed claims (not just active cases) because each filed claim triggers compliance review. Parties and attorneys can determine counts through eCCB searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and Federal Rules of Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule addresses, in discussion and regulatory text, the applicability of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and the Federal Rules of Evidence to CCB proceedings as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office balanced minimizing complexity with ensuring sufficient procedural safeguards; applicability is tailored so parties (including pro se) are not overwhelmed by full federal procedural complexity, but the rules allow enough rigor to permit just determinations. (See 37 CFR provisions and final regulatory text for specific applications.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Written requests and other filings (formatting, timing, eCCB forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rules and final revisions specify procedures for filing written requests and other submissions to the CCB, including formatting and timing requirements, and provide standardized/expandable eCCB forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revisions in the final rule specify the formatting and timing of party submissions to establish consistency and streamline proceedings; certain requests (e.g., intervention) will be handled via simple eCCB forms. If electronic submission is not feasible, parties may contact the Office for special instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCB will use scheduling orders to manage proceedings, including setting deadlines for filings, discovery, testimony, and hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling orders are intended to keep proceedings efficient and predictable while allowing flexibility for complexity when inherent in the factual context. The Office aims to streamline requirements where appropriate to reduce burdens on pro se parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amending claims and counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations govern amending claims and counterclaims, including permitting amendments with leave of the CCB in specified circumstances (e.g., after opt-out period where CCB's leave is required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments suggested clarifying amendments after opt-out; the Office noted existing regulation already allows leave in certain circumstances. The CCB will balance amendment rights against fairness to parties and docket management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation and severance
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCB may consolidate related claims and sever portions of proceedings where appropriate to efficient management of its docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation/severance rules accommodate efficiency and fairness; the Office expects to apply these tools where case overlap or complexity warrants them while protecting parties' ability to present claims and defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement encouragement and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office encourages voluntary settlement and includes provisions and flexibility for parties to settle claims during CCB proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters praised proposals to encourage settlement; the CCB's procedures and scheduling are intended to facilitate settlement where appropriate, and provisions address recordation and effect of settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Records and publication of determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule addresses records and publication: determinations of the CCB will be available to the public, and the eCCB will allow searches of information about parties and attorneys appearing before the CCB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will allow for redactions where appropriate and follow statutory limits, but generally CCB determinations and orders (including those related to bad faith) are publicly accessible. Users should verify official content against the PDF on govinfo.gov when conducting legal research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders (confidentiality / ESI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protective orders may be issued at the request of any party to protect confidential or sensitive material (including ESI) produced during discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed regulations note protective orders apply “[a]t the request of any party.” The Office will limit discovery of ESI and other burdensome requests through protective orders and other discovery constraints to balance access to information with cost and complexity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office contemplates and supports the use of standardized interrogatories (CCB-issued interrogatories) to streamline discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters (e.g., Amazon, Authors Guild, SFWA) strongly approved standardized interrogatories and standard document requests; the Office sees standardized forms as a tool to make discovery efficient and accessible for pro se parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for admission (limited use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCB permits limited requests for admission as part of streamlined discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters praised limited requests for admission as a cost-effective discovery tool; the Board will shape rules to ensure requests are narrowly tailored to relevant matters to avoid overbroad discovery disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of documents (scope and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Document production is permitted but will be limited to items that are relevant, probative, and likely to impact the outcome of the case; limitations on discovery scope are intended to avoid fishing expeditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged limits to avoid burdensome discovery; the Office adopted rules to constrain discovery to relevant materials and to limit ESI burdens. Standardized document requests are favored to reduce complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions (generally disfavored; good-cause standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions are generally not permitted in small-claims style CCB proceedings and are a costly discovery tool; depositions may be allowed only upon a showing of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters (e.g., Amazon) requested clarifying depositions are permitted only upon a showing of good cause; the Office recognizes depositions' cost and will limit them accordingly consistent with statutory directives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert disclosure and expert costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations address expert disclosure requirements and the potential for significant expert costs in copyright matters (e.g., musicologists, computer forensics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office is mindful of expert cost implications and discovery burdens; rules will constrain expert discovery and consider proportionality, while allowing necessary expert evidence when probative of issues in dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written testimony and submission of exhibits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's rules describe requirements for written testimony, documentary evidence, and witness/party statements to support claims and defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters asked the Handbook to explain exactly what to include in written testimony (documentary evidence, witness and party statements) and provide lists of topics, sample documents, and forms. The rule also limits how exhibits not submitted as part of written testimony may be used at hearings (e.g., impeachment/rehabilitation only, and copies must be distributed beforehand unless the Board directs otherwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearings (attendance and procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations govern hearings before the CCB, including procedures for witness testimony, admission of evidence, and attendance limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office may impose attendance limitations initially and monitor whether those should be eased as CCB operations normalize. Hearing procedures aim to balance simplicity for pro se parties with fair opportunity to develop and present evidence; the Board will monitor whether attendance limitations should be adjusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-determination review, rehearing, and Register's review
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules provide for post-determination rehearing and the Register's review of CCB determinations, including the Register's ability to remand for reconsideration and issue an amended final determination that is not subject to further CCB or Register review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule describes procedural paths for rehearing and internal review consistent with 17 U.S.C. provisions; parties should consult the regulatory text for deadlines and grounds for rehearing or review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller-claims procedures and solicitation of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule describes procedures for 'smaller claims' and solicits public comments on the regulations governing these proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office specifically sought comment on the smaller-claims procedures; it will consider public feedback and may adjust these rules. The CCB Handbook and eCCB will include user-friendly guidance tailored to smaller-claims practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection and ongoing review of regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will monitor how regulations function as the CCB begins hearing claims and will collect data and potentially promulgate additional CASE Act regulations or adjust limits and discovery rules based on experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CASE Act requires a future study on CCB operations; the Office expects to review fee structures and procedural rules periodically and encourages ex parte feedback via the Office's meeting processes to address unforeseen issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and timing consistency for filings
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule revises procedures to specify the formatting and timing of party submissions to establish consistency and streamline proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters raised concerns about formatting and timing for filings (including filings raising or responding to bad-faith assertions); the Office addressed these concerns in the final rule to create consistent practices across proceedings and to assist pro se parties in complying with procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCB Handbook and eCCB as implementation tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will publish a CCB Handbook and operate a user-friendly electronic filing system (eCCB) to guide parties through all stages of CCB proceedings with plain-language instructions, prompts, and fillable forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Handbook will not override statute or regulations but will provide practical, plain-English guidance (including examples of bad-faith conduct, sample forms, and lists of topics for written testimony). eCCB will simplify filings, enable searches of filings/parties/attorneys, and provide fillable forms for interventions, discovery, and other common requests; CCB staff will be available to assist users who run into difficulty.
